The strongest argument for remote work as the default is that many office jobs are organized around information rather than location. Remote work can save commute time, widen hiring pools, support workers with disabilities or caregiving responsibilities, and let employees live in more affordable places. It can also reduce office costs for employers and give workers more control over focused time.

The strongest argument against making it the default is that coordination, mentorship, trust-building, and informal learning often become harder. Managers may struggle to notice overload or onboard new employees well. Junior workers can miss the ambient learning that happens when questions are easy to ask. Cities also feel the effects: downtown businesses, transit systems, and commercial real estate can suffer when office districts empty out.

A sensible conclusion is that remote work is powerful but uneven. It works best when teams design communication deliberately, invest in onboarding, and reserve in-person time for collaboration that genuinely benefits from presence rather than habit.
